h1: Gruit: the herbal beer brewed before hops took over
title: Gruit: The Herbal Beer Before Hops | Craft Beer School
desc: What gruit is, which herbs went into it, why hops replaced it in medieval Europe and what a modern gruit tastes like in the glass.
teaser: For centuries Europe's beer was bittered with bog myrtle and yarrow, not hops. Then the rules changed.
standfirst: Hops feel like they have always been part of beer. They have not. For a long stretch of history the bitter, aromatic part of a pint came from a bundle of herbs called gruit. The story of how it vanished is part botany, part tax policy.
sections:
Malt on its own makes a sweet, heavy drink that spoils quickly. Brewers have always wanted something to balance that sweetness and help the beer keep. In much of medieval northern Europe, in the Low Countries and along the Rhine, the answer was gruit: a mixture of dried herbs added to the wort or the fermenting beer.

No single recipe existed. The most commonly recorded herbs are bog myrtle (also called sweet gale), yarrow and marsh rosemary. Brewers and gruit makers added others depending on region and season, from juniper and caraway to heather. Some mixes were closely guarded. That secrecy turns out to matter.
Gruit was a tax as much as a recipe

In many towns brewers could not make their own herb mix. The right to sell gruit, often called the gruit right, belonged to a local lord, a bishop or the town itself. Brewers had to buy the mixture from the holder of that right, which made gruit a convenient way to tax beer. Every batch brewed paid its share through the herb bag.

This is why the switch to hops was a political fight as well as a matter of taste. A brewer who used hops instead stepped outside the gruit system. The people collecting the money noticed.

Hops had two practical advantages. Their bitter acids are mildly antibacterial, so hopped beer stayed sound for longer and could travel. That suited the trading towns of northern Germany, whose hopped beers were shipped across the Baltic and the North Sea. Over roughly the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries hopped beer spread west and south. Gruit rights were either converted into taxes on hops or quietly dropped.

Bavaria's beer purity law of 1516, which allowed only barley, hops and water (yeast was not yet understood), is often quoted as the moment herbs were pushed out of German beer. It was one law in one duchy, but it captured the direction of travel. By the time the hop arrived in English brewing it met resistance too: ale meant the unhopped drink and beer meant the hopped one, a distinction that took a long time to blur.

Modern brewers who make gruit usually work from historical lists rather than a single surviving recipe, so expect variety. Bog myrtle gives a resinous, slightly medicinal bitterness that sits somewhere between bay leaf and eucalyptus. Yarrow is grassy and bitter. Heather and juniper lean floral and piney. Without hop bitterness the beer often tastes softer and rounder, with the herbs adding perfume rather than a sharp bitter finish.

One honest warning from the brewhouse: some historical gruit herbs contain compounds that are not safe in quantity. Marsh rosemary in particular is treated with caution by modern brewers. Anyone making gruit should use food-grade herbs from a reputable supplier and keep doses small. Historical does not mean harmless.

If the idea of herbs in beer sounds odd, think of a witbier with coriander and orange peel, or the ginger, tulsi and black pepper beers some Indian brewpubs pour. These are cousins of gruit in spirit: the brewer reaching for local aromatics to give the beer character. Our guide to brewing with Indian spices covers how much to use and when to add it, which is exactly the question a gruit brewer faces.

The difference is that most spiced beers today still carry hops for bitterness and stability. A true gruit leans on herbs alone, which makes it more fragile. Brewers keep it fresh, serve it young and avoid long warm storage, a sensible rule in an Indian summer anyway.

Gruit is rare on any tap list. When you see one, order a small pour and taste it slowly. Smell first, then notice where the bitterness lands, at the front of the tongue or the back and how long it lasts. Comparing it side by side with a lightly hopped beer is the quickest way to understand what hops changed. It is also a good exercise in tasting without the reference points you are used to, the skill our guide to tasting beer starts with.

Gruit will never replace the hop. It is a reminder that the familiar shape of beer was a choice, made by brewers, merchants and tax collectors and that a different choice once produced a different drink.
faqs: Yes, by a small number of craft brewers, usually as a special or seasonal release. Each brewer works from historical herb lists, so two gruits can taste quite different.
A traditional gruit does not. The bitterness and aroma come from herbs such as bog myrtle and yarrow. Some modern versions add a small amount of hops for stability.
Why did brewers stop using gruit?
Hopped beer kept and travelled better. Hops spread with the trade in northern European beer. The gruit right was also a tax, so the change involved money and politics as well as flavour.
